findings_qualitative.value: A pair of symmetric, trailing m=2 spiral arms (NE and SW) is detected in the 343 GHz dust continuum of the embedded Class I protostellar disk HH 111 VLA 1, extending from ~40 au to ~160 au.

evidence.quote: Figure 2c shows the difference map, which clearly shows a pair of symmetric spiral structures labeled “NE” and “SW” extending from within ∼ 0 [′′] . 1 (40 au) of the central source to the outer edge of the disk.
The spiral structures trail the rotation of the disk measured in molecular lines [5] .

findings_qualitative.value: The companion source HH 111 VLA 2 is spatially resolved for the first time into a ~25.6 au disklike structure nearly orthogonal to the VLA 1 disk and roughly perpendicular to the HH 121 jet.

evidence.quote: The emission around the VLA 2 source is spatially resolved for the first time, appearing as a disklike structure, with a Gaussian deconvolved size (diameter) of 0 [′′] . 064 (25.6 au) along the major axis at position angle 118.3 [◦] .
Note that the VLA 2 disklike structure is nearly orthogonal to the VLA 1 disk, indicating the two components of this wide protobinary system are strongly misaligned.

claims.hypothesis: Symmetric m=2 spiral arms can form in an embedded Class I protostellar disk driven into gravitational instability by rapid envelope accretion.
claims.experiment: High-resolution (0.04 arcsec) ALMA 343 GHz continuum imaging, deprojection and annular average subtraction, spiral shape fitting, and radiative transfer disk modeling of HH 111 VLA 1.
claims.result: Detected a pair of symmetric trailing spiral arms from ~40 to 160 au with pitch angles ~13-16 deg; flared disk modeling yields a disk mass of 0.33-0.50 M_sun (22-33% of stellar mass) and Toomre Q < 1.5 beyond 100 au.
claims.finding: The spiral structures and high disk mass (low Toomre Q) support global gravitational instability fed by envelope accretion as the driver of the spiral arms.

evidence.quote: Additionally, the disk is massive, with Toomre’s Q parameter near unity in the outer parts where the spiral structures are detected, supporting the notion that

Therefore, the resulting Toomre’s Q value is less than 1.5 for the outer part of the disk with a radius ∼> 100 au (Supplementary Figure 3), further supporting the possibility of global non-axisymmetric GI as the driver for the spiral arms [33] .

claims.hypothesis: The spiral arms in HH 111 VLA 1 can be distinguished between logarithmic (GI-driven) and Archimedean (planet/companion-driven) shapes using their radial pitch angle profile.
claims.experiment: Fit radial emission peak positions of the NE and SW spiral arms with both logarithmic and Archimedean spiral models using nonlinear least squares.
claims.result: The SW arm is slightly better fitted by a logarithmic spiral (chi^2 = 2.07 vs 3.77), whereas the NE arm is slightly better fitted by an Archimedean spiral (chi^2 = 1.41 vs 2.88).
claims.finding: Neither spiral shape fits both arms best at current resolution and sensitivity; both GI and an embedded companion remain possible based on shape alone.

evidence.quote: Based on the χ [2] values, it appears that the SW arm is slightly better fitted by a logarithmic shape, while the NE arm is slightly better fitted by an Archimedean shape.
Since neither shape fits both arms best, higher-resolution and deeper observations are needed to better distinguish these two possibilities.

claims.hypothesis: HH 111 VLA 2 is a disk system that drives the HH 121 jet and forms a misaligned protobinary with VLA 1.
claims.experiment: Resolve the 343 GHz continuum emission around HH 111 VLA 2 at 0.04 arcsec resolution and measure its size and position angle.
claims.result: VLA 2 is spatially resolved with a Gaussian deconvolved diameter of 0.064 arcsec (25.6 au) at PA 118.3 deg, roughly perpendicular to HH 121 and nearly orthogonal to the VLA 1 disk.
claims.finding: VLA 2 has a compact disklike structure that likely drives the HH 121 jet and is strongly misaligned with the VLA 1 disk.

evidence.quote: The emission around the VLA 2 source is spatially resolved for the first time, appearing as a disklike structure, with a Gaussian deconvolved size (diameter) of 0 [′′] . 064 (25.6 au) along the major axis at position angle 118.3 [◦] .
Note that the VLA 2 disklike structure is nearly orthogonal to the VLA 1 disk, indicating the two components of this wide protobinary system are strongly misaligned.

why_this_method.value: Subtracted an annularly averaged map from the deprojected continuum map to reveal faint (5-20% contrast) spiral arms on top of the bright axisymmetric disk profile, and added outer geometric thinning to the hydrostatic disk model to match the observed thinning at the outer disk edge.

evidence.quote: In order to better see the spirals, we first made an annularly averaged map of the continuum (see Figure 2b) then subtracted it from the deprojected map [9] .

With this scale height, increasing monotonically in radius, we failed to fit the observed thinning of the disk near its outer edge. Thus, as in HH 212, we assume the disk to be geometrically thinner near its outer edge.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Spiral arms driven by an internal planet/companion at ~40 au, an external companion (VLA 2 at ~1200 au projected separation), or a putative ~1 M_sun companion at ~186 au inferred from jet wiggling.

evidence.quote: The spirals in the VLA 1 disk could instead be raised by a planet or companion. Our fit of the Archimedean form to the spirals indicates the pitch angle increases inwards to ∼ 40 au (0 [′′] . 1), where we would thus expect the planet or companion to be located and to clear a gap in the disk.
One possibility is VLA 2, but we believe this is not likely to be the driver because the disk of VLA 1 is highly inclined with respect to the plane of the sky, being nearly edge-on.

Another possibility is a putative stellar companion of ∼ 1M ⊙, inferred to lie at a distance of ∼ 186 au from VLA 1 based on the wiggling of the HH 111 jet and counterjet [35] . However, such a massive young star should have a disk detectable with our sensitive ALMA continuum observation if it is at an evolutionary stage similar to that of VLA 1, yet nothing is seen.

limitations_admitted.value: Inner barlike structures connecting to the spiral arms may be artifacts from deprojecting the spatially unresolved central core.

evidence.quote: Near the central source, two barlike structures connect to the inner ends of the spiral structures. Since they are not clearly seen in the original map, these could be artifacts of the deprojection of the central region, which is spatially unresolved in the observation.

limitations_admitted.value: Current angular resolution and sensitivity cannot definitively distinguish between logarithmic and Archimedean spiral shapes or detect a narrow planet-carved gap in the massive disk.

evidence.quote: Since neither shape fits both arms best, higher-resolution and deeper observations are needed to better distinguish these two possibilities.

However, since the disk seems to be too massive for a planet to open a gap detectable at the current resolution [34], observations at higher resolution are needed to search for a gap and check for this scenario.

limitations_admitted.value: The dust opacity spectral index beta is uncertain, which affects the derived disk mass and Toomre Q parameter, and the radiative transfer model is axisymmetric and neglects self-gravity in the vertical scale height.

evidence.quote: Since the dust opacity is uncertain, further observations are needed to confirm the instability and check whether the inner part is also gravitationally unstable.
However, in our model, the Q parameter is of order unity or larger, and the effect of self-gravity on the scale height is moderate (at most a factor of 2).

referee_caveats_inferred: Deprojecting a highly inclined (axis inclined ~18 deg to plane of sky, i.e., ~72 deg inclination) flared disk with finite vertical thickness (h/R ~ 0.17) using a simple 2D planar stretch can introduce azimuthal projection distortions.
Spiral peak positions were measured by fitting Gaussians 'by eye' along radial cuts, which introduces subjective uncertainty.
The disk is partly optically thick at 343 GHz along the major axis, making surface density and Toomre Q estimates sensitive to the assumed temperature structure and dust opacity.
